title: Polyamine metabolism and immune related genes as prognostic features in breast cancer: a novel risk model approach

sections.abstract:
The biological role of polyamine metabolism-related genes (PMRGs) in breast cancer (BRCA) through immune mediation is not well understood. Consequently, this study aimed to explore the prognostic features connected to PMRGs and immune-related genes (IRGs) in BRCA via bioinformatics analysis.

We analyzed The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-BRCA and GSE20685 datasets. Differential expression analysis revealed differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in TCGA-BRCA, which intersected with 1,793 IRGs and 59 PMRGs to identify candidate genes. A least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox regression model was used to screen prognostic genes, which were then used to develop a risk model. This model was validated in both datasets. A nomogram was constructed using independent prognostic factors from univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses to predict BRCA patient survival. The immune microenvironment landscape and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) results were also characterized.

Among 9,558 DEGs, 1,793 IRGs, and 59 PMRGs, 10 candidate genes were identified, with PSME2 , PSMB8 , and PSMD14 selected as prognostic genes. The risk model stratified BRCA patients into high- and low-risk groups, with high-risk patients showing worse survival according to Kaplan-Meier analysis. The nomogram, which is based on the pathological stage and risk score, accurately predicts patient viability. High-risk patients have poor immune responses. GSEA revealed immune-related pathway involvement. PSME2 and PSMB8 were upregulated in the control samples, whereas PSMD14 was increased in the BRCA samples. The CCK8 assay results indicated that PSMD14 significantly promotes the proliferation of BRCA cells.

PMRGs and IRGs, specifically PSME2 , PSMB8 , and PSMD14 , are potential prognostic markers in BRCA. A risk model and nomogram based on these genes were developed to assess BRCA prognosis effectively. These tools can improve the prognostic assessment of BRCA patients.

Keywords: Breast cancer (BRCA), bioinformatics analysis, prognostic genes, nomogram model, risk mode
sections.introduction:
Breast cancer (BRCA) represents the most common form of malignant cancer affecting women, with an estimated 2.3 million new cases and 666,000 fatalities documented in global cancer statistics for the year 2022 ( 1 ). The histopathological classification of BRCA is predominantly based on the evaluation of progesterone receptor (PR), estrogen receptor (ER), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) expression. This classification framework includes the luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like, and normal-like subtypes of BRCA ( 2 ). Currently, the primary treatments for BRCA include radiation therapy, hormone therapy, chemotherapy, and surgical intervention. Additionally, various drug combinations and targeted therapies have demonstrated efficacy in the management of BRCA ( 3 ). Although the mortality rate associated with BRCA has declined, prognostication remains challenging owing to the heterogeneous nature of the disease ( 4 ). The existing predictive factors are insufficient, underscoring the need for novel predictors to improve prognostic accuracy.

The immune system plays a crucial role in inhibiting cancer progression. However, its efficacy can be compromised within the tumor microenvironment (TME) due to elements such as checkpoint signaling pathways and immunosuppressive cytokines ( 5 ). Research has indicated that immune-related genes (IRGs) are correlated with BRCA prognosis ( 6 ). These IRGs can either facilitate or inhibit tumor development through their interactions with immune cells and tumor cells within the TME. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are immune cells that penetrate the TME and are correlated with improved prognostic outcomes in patients with BRCA. Elevated TIL levels suggest a more vigorous immune response, which can be exploited for therapeutic purposes ( 7 ). Among the IRGs extensively investigated in BRCA, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) is of particular importance. PD-L1 interacts with the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) receptor on immune cells, resulting in the suppression of T-cell activity and facilitating the evasion of immune surveillance by cancer cells. Numerous clinical trials have validated the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in the treatment of specific BRCA subtypes characterized by elevated PD-L1 expression ( 8 ). The involvement of immune-suppressive cytokines, notably interleukin-6 (IL-6), in BRCA pathophysiology has also been the subject of extensive research. IL-6, a proinflammatory cytokine, is known to facilitate tumor progression, angiogenesis, and metastasis through its ability to modulate the immune response ( 9 ). In addition to these well-studied IRGs, HSPA8 is an oncogene of which its function has been recently discovered to be mediated by histone chaperones (HCs), which can promote the metastasis and invasion of BRCA tumors ( 10 ). Consequently, the identification and comprehensive understanding of IRGs associated with BRCA are crucial for advancing therapeutic strategies and improving prognostic outcomes.

Polyamines, which are ubiquitous polycationic molecules essential for normal cellular function, are elevated in the majority of human cancers ( 11 ). In the context of BRCA, the polyamine biosynthetic pathway is upregulated, leading to a marked increase in polyamine levels in tumor tissue compared with those in normal epithelial breast tissue ( 12 ). These elevated levels of polyamines and associated metabolic enzymes are correlated with poor prognostic outcomes in both breast and colorectal cancers ( 13 , 14 ). Similarly, various prognostic indicators of BRCA, such as tumor size and histological grade, are associated with increased polyamine content within tumors, highlighting the critical role of polyamines in BRCA development and progression ( 15 ). Despite the association between elevated polyamine levels and poor prognosis in patients with BRCA, researchers have not yet determined whether BRCA cells with different hormone receptor statuses rely similarly on polyamines for continued proliferation. IRGs have the potential to contribute to cancer development, whereas elevated levels of polyamine metabolic enzymes have been linked to unfavorable prognoses in patients with breast and colorectal cancers. However, the precise biological role of genes associated with polyamine metabolism in BRCA, particularly through immune-mediated mechanisms, remains inadequately understood.

In this study, we analyzed sequencing data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-BRCA dataset, accessed via the University of California Santa Cruz (UCSC) Xena database, and the GSE20685 dataset, retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Using bioinformatics methodologies, such as differential expression analysis and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-Cox regression analysis, this research examined the prognostic significance of the immune response and polyamine metabolism in BRCA. The objective of this study was to improve prognostic prediction markers for patients affected by this condition. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD reporting checklist (available at https://tcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tcr-2024-2505/rc ).
sections.methods:
The BRCA-related datasets TCGA-BRCA and GSE20685 were acquired from two public databases: the UCSC Xena ( https://xenabrowser.net/ ) and the GEO ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ), respectively. Different datasets from various platforms were selected because these two datasets can complement each other and are helpful for enhancing the universality of the research results. In total, 113 normal tissue samples and 1,082 BRCA tumor tissue samples with complete survival and clinical information in the TCGA-BRCA dataset were retained. The GSE20685 dataset included chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) data from 327 BRCA patients with survival information. A total of 1,793 IRGs and 59 polyamine metabolism-related genes (PMRGs) were identified from the Immunology Database and Analysis Portal (ImmPort, https://www.immport.org ) and Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB, https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/ ), respectively.

To obtain differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between BRCA patients and controls, differential expression analysis was performed based on the TCGA-BRCA dataset utilizing the R package ‘DESeq2’ (Ver. 1.38.0) ( 16 ) (|Log 2 fold change (FC) |>0.5, adj. P<0.05), and the same data were obtained in normalized FPKM format, which brought the data closer to a normal distribution and made it more suitable for statistical analysis. The intersection of 1,793 IRGs and 59 PMRGs overlapped with the DEGs to identify candidate genes. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analyses were subsequently performed via the R package ‘clusterProfiler’ (Ver. 4.7.1) ( 17 ), which was utilized for investigating the underlying functions of candidate genes (adj. P<0.05). A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was created to reveal the relationships among candidate genes at the protein level via the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes (STRING, https://www.string-db.org/ ) database, with a threshold of interaction score >0.4.

To predict the risk of developing BRCA, a risk model was built. First, based on 1,082 BRCA tumor tissue samples in the TCGA-BRCA dataset, the ‘coxph’ function in the R package ‘survival’ (Ver. 3.5-3) ( 18 ) and the R package ‘glmnet’ (Ver. 4.1-4) ( 19 ) were utilized for univariate Cox regression analysis (HR≠1, P<0.05) and LASSO regression analysis, respectively, to screen prognostic genes. The risk model we built was based on the coefficients of the genes obtained from the LASSO regression, and the risk scoring equation was as follows: risk score = ∑ i = 1 n coef ( gene i ) × expr ( gene i ) , where ‘coef’ refers to the regression coefficients, and ‘expr’ represents the relative expression levels of prognostic genes.

The BRCA patients in the TCGA-BRCA dataset were subsequently sorted into high- and low-risk cohorts in accordance with the optimum cutoff value. Using the optimum cutoff value can maximize the value of sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing between high-risk and low-risk groups. In addition, a Kaplan-Meier (K-M) survival curve was drawn to estimate the survival discrepancies of BRCA patients between the two risk cohorts (P<0.05). To further evaluate the effectiveness of the risk model, we created a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve [area under the ROC curve (AUC) ≥0.6)]. Additionally, the risk model established based on the TCGA-BRCA dataset was verified with the GSE20685 dataset. Similarly, the BRCA patients in the GSE20685 dataset were categorized into two risk cohorts via the optimum cutoff value, and assessment of survival discrepancies among patients in the two risk cohorts and evaluation of the risk model were subsequently conducted with the GSE20685 dataset.

With the aim of investigating the effect of prognostic genes on the prognosis of patients in different clinicopathological subgroups, the discrepancies in risk scores between subgroups according to age and pathologic T, N and M stages were assessed via Wilcoxon’s test (P<0.05).

To predict the prognosis of BRCA patients, we developed a nomogram model via the R package ‘rms’ (Ver. 6.5-0) ( 18 ). In detail, age; pathologic T, N and M stages; and risk scores were incorporated into univariate (P<0.05) and multivariate Cox regression analyses (P<0.05) to screen independent prognostic factors for nomogram modeling. The predictive value of the nomogram model was reflected in the survival probabilities of patients with BRCA at 1-, 2-, and 3-year. In addition, calibration and ROC curves were drawn, and decision curve analysis (DCA) was used to evaluate the predictive ability of the nomogram model.

To understand the impact of prognostic genes on the progression of BRCA, Wilcoxon’s test was used to compare the differences in the expression levels of prognostic genes between BRCA patients and controls in the TCGA-BRCA dataset (P<0.05).

With the aim of identifying functional genes between the two risk cohorts, differential expression analysis was performed to compute the Log2FC of DEGs between two risk cohorts, and genes sorted by Log2FC from largest to smallest were selected for GSEA. GSEA was implemented by the ‘clusterProfiler’ package in R with ‘c2.cp.kegg.v2023.1.Hs.symbols.gmt’ retrieved from MSigDB as a background gene set (adj. P<0.05).

To characterize the tumor mutation conditions between the two risk cohorts, the R package ‘maftools’ (Ver. 2.14.0) ( 20 ) was employed for differential analysis of somatic mutations between the two risk cohorts by calculating the tumor mutation burden (TMB) score of each patient in the TCGA-BRCA dataset.

In addition, the sensitivity of patients to 138 common chemotherapy drugs in the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer database (GDSC, https://www.cancerrxgene.org/ ) was assessed. Using the TCGA-BRCA dataset, the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 138 drugs was estimated and compared between the two risk cohorts (adj. P<0.05).

By using a reporter, immune cell infiltration (ICI) plays a crucial role in BRCA progression ( 20 ); therefore, the association between the two risk cohorts and the immune microenvironment was further evaluated. The abundance of 22 immune cells between the two risk cohorts was estimated through the CIBERSORT algorithm, and discrepant immune cells were identified (P<0.05). Next, the results were visualized using the R packages ‘ggplot2’ (Ver. 3.4.1), ‘pheatmap’ (Ver. 1.0.12) and ‘ComplexHeatmap’ (Ver. 2.14.0) to visualize the results. Furthermore, the correlations among discrepant immune cells were explored via Spearman’s correlation analysis, as were the relationships between discrepant immune cells and prognostic genes (|R|>0.3, P<0.05).

With the goal of understanding the immunotherapy effect on BRCA patients in the two risk cohorts, the discrepancies in the expression levels of 48 immune checkpoints between the two risk cohorts were analyzed through Wilcoxon’s test with a threshold of P<0.05. Additionally, the relationships between prognostic genes and different immune checkpoints were revealed. The tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) score, dysfunction score and exclusion score were sourced from the TIDE database ( http://tide.dfci.harvard.edu/ ). The discrepancies in the three scores between the two risk cohorts were examined by Wilcoxon’s test with P<0.05.

RNAs from 23 pairs of tissue samples, comprising 23 BRCA samples and 23 control paracancerous tissue samples, were collected from The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (as revised in 2013). All participants provided written informed consents, and the study received ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University (Approval No. 2024YS060). Total RNA was isolated from the tissue samples according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Reverse transcription of messenger RNA (mRNA) was performed using the SweScript First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit, and qPCR was conducted using the SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix. The primer sequences are listed in Table S1 . The mRNA levels were normalized to those of GAPDH. The relevant gene expression was calculated via the 2 −ΔΔCt method, and the p value was calculated via GraphPad Prism 6.

Fresh tumor samples were fixed in neutral buffered formalin for 24 hours at room temperature, followed by embedding and processing according to standard protocols. Sections were deparaffinized using graded ethanol solutions and rehydrated. After a 30-minute antigen retrieval procedure using antigen retrieval solution, the sections were stained with PSME2, PSMB8 and PSMD14. The stained sections were then scanned by Servicebio.

BRCA cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 50,000–100,000 cells per well and cultured overnight to reach 50–70% confluency. Each siRNA (siRNA#1: GGCAUUAAUUCAUGGACUA; siRNA#2: GAUGGUUGUUGGUUGGUAU) was diluted to a working concentration of 20 µM in nuclease-free water. For transfection, 5 µL of Lipofectamine 2000 was mixed with 100 µL of Opti-MEM I medium and incubated for 5 minutes at room temperature. Then, 50 nM of each siRNA was added to the mixture, bringing the total volume to 200 µL. After a 20-minute incubation at room temperature, the siRNA-lipid complex was added dropwise to each well containing cells in Opti-MEM I medium. Cells were incubated at 37 ℃ with 5% CO 2 for 48 hours to allow for PSMD14 knockdown. Post-transfection, cells were processed for RNA extraction to confirm knockdown efficiency.

The proliferation of PSMD14 knockdown breast cell lines was assessed using the CCK8 assay. Each cell type was seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1,000 cells per well, with three replicates per condition. Cells were either continuously treated with 0.5 µM of the drug or left untreated, and blank wells were also set up. Proliferation was measured every 24 hours over a period of 3 days. At each designated time point, 10 µL of CCK8 reagent was added to each well, followed by incubation at 37 ℃ for 3 hours. The absorbance was then measured using a microplate reader at 450 nm. Cell proliferation curves were generated and analyzed using GraphPad Prism 6.

Bioinformatics analysis was implemented through R software (Ver. 4.3.1) in this study. A P or adj. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant unless otherwise noted.
sections.results:
A total of 9,558 DEGs were acquired via differential expression analysis, including 5,923 upregulated and 3,635 downregulated genes in the BRCA group ( Figure 1A,1B ). In total, 23 immune-polyamine metabolism-related genes (I-PMRGs) were produced by overlapping 1,793 IRGs and 59 PMRGs ( Figure 1C ), which intersected with 9,558 DEGs, retaining 10 candidate genes ( Figure 1D ). Furthermore, GO revealed that these candidate genes were enriched in 25 GO-biological processes (BPs), 13 GO-cellular components (CCs) and 13 GO-molecular functions (MFs), and these GO items involved biological processes related to protein catabolic processes and proteolysis ( Figure 1E ). In addition, candidate genes involved in protein metabolism, abnormal protein deposition or treatment during the onset and progression of disease were associated with 10 KEGG signaling pathways ( Figure 1F ). In conclusion, the functions of the candidate genes were associated with protein metabolism. The interactions of candidate genes were exhibited in the PPI network, and the close interactions among them formed 45 interaction pairs, such as PSME1-PSME2 and PSMD14-PSMB8 ( Figure 1G ).

Identification of immune- and polyamine metabolism-related genes. (A) Volcano plot of DEGs in the BRCA dataset. (B) Heatmap of DEGs in the BRCA dataset. (C) Venn map acquisition of 23 intersection genes of IRGs and PMRGs. (D) Venn map acquisition of 10 intersection genes of DEGs and I-PMRGs. (E) Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of 10 intersecting genes. (F) KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of 10 intersecting genes. (G) Construction of a PPI network for 10 intersecting genes. BRCA, breast cancer; DEGs, differentially expressed genes; FC, fold change; I-PMRGs, immune-polyamine metabolism-related genes; IRGs, immune-related genes; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes; PMRGs, polyamine metabolism-related genes.

Overall, univariate Cox regression analysis revealed that four genes ( PSME2 , PSME1 , PSMB8 and PSMD14 ) were associated with the prognosis of BRCA patients, of which PSME2 , PSME1 and PSMB8 were protective factors against BRCA (HR <1) and PSMD14 was a risk factor for BRCA (HR >1) ( Figure 2A ). These 4 genes were subjected to LASSO regression analysis, and PSME2 , PSMB8 and PSMD14 were selected as prognostic genes when the model error reached a minimum ( Figure 2B,2C ). The LASSO regression coefficient of each prognostic gene is presented in Table 1 , and the risk scoring equation was as follows: risk score = PSME2×(−0.36229220) + PSMB8×(−0.06306154) + PSMD14×(0.43677028).

Construction of a risk model by LASSO and Cox regression analysis in the training group. (A) The forest plot for univariate Cox analysis. (B,C) LASSO regression was used to determine the optimal outcome λ values. (D,E) Distribution of the risk score and survival status between low-/high-risk patients in the training set. (F) Kaplan-Meier survival analysis between low- and high-risk subgroups of patients in the training set. (G) Time-dependent ROC curve analysis of the training set. (H) Boxplot of differences in risk scores across clinical indicators in the TCGA cohort. AUC, area under the curve; CI, confidence interval; LASSO, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator; ROC, receiver operating characteristic; TCGA, The Cancer Genome Atlas.

LASSO, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.

Based on the risk model built using the three prognostic genes, the risk scores of 1,082 BRCA tumor tissue samples were computed, splitting the BRCA patients in the TCGA-BRCA dataset into 390 high-risk patients and 692 low-risk patients ( Figure 2D ). High-risk patients had a higher mortality rate ( Figure 2E ). Additionally, a greater survival probability of high-risk patients was demonstrated via K-M survival curves ( Figure 2F ). Notably, the credible prediction ability of the risk model was proven by the ROC curve, with AUCs of 0.61, 0.61 and 0.64 at 1-, 2-, and 3-year, respectively ( Figure 2G ). Furthermore, to ensure the universality of the risk model, the 327 BRCA patients in the GSE20685 dataset were separated into 99 and 228 high- and low-risk patients, respectively ( Figure S1A,S1B ), and the outcomes of the K-M survival curves were in line with those in the TCGA-BRCA dataset ( Figure S1C ). The universality of the risk model was verified in the GSE20685 dataset because the AUCs at 1-, 2-, and 3-year were 0.76, 0.63 and 0.61, respectively ( Figure S1D ). Subsequent analysis of the differences in risk scores between different clinicopathological subgroups revealed that the risk scores of patients with pathologic N1 stage disease were significantly greater than those of patients with pathologic N3 stage disease ( Figure 2H ).

To better understand the prognosis of BRCA patients, independent prognostic analysis was performed. First, the risk score, N stage, M stage and pathologic T stage were identified as independent prognostic factors ( Figure 3A,3B ). A nomogram model for predicting the viability of BRCA patients was created based on independent prognostic factors. As the total score increased, the 1-, 2- and 3-year viability of BRCA patients also increased ( Figure 3C ). Furthermore, the nomogram model’s predictive performance was effectively demonstrated through calibration curves, which revealed a higher overlap ratio of viability at 1-, 2-, and 3-year with the reference line ( Figure 3D ). The DCA curve indicated that the net benefits of the nomogram model outweighed those of the other separate factors, suggesting that the model was effective ( Figure 3E ). In addition, the AUCs of 1-, 2-, and 3-year survival were all above 0.7, suggesting that the nomogram exhibited strong predictive performance ( Figure 3F ). Further analysis of prognostic gene expression revealed higher expression of PSME2, PSMB8 and PSMD14 in the BRCA group than in the control group ( Figure 4A ).

Construction and evaluation of a nomogram based on independent prognostic indicators of BRCA. (A,B) Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were used to screen the independent prognostic indicators of BRCA from the clinical features of BRCA and the risk score. (C) Construction of a nomogram in conjunction with variables that independently predict BRCA prognosis. (D) Calibration plot of the nomogram. (E) Decision curve analysis for the BRCA prognosis-related index and nomogram. (F) AUC for predicting 1-, 3-, and 5-year overall survival for comparing the accuracy of various prognostic characteristics. AUC, area under the curve; BRCA, breast cancer; CI, confidence interval; ROC, receiver operating characteristic.

KEGG and mutation chemotherapeutic drug sensitivity analyses. (A) The expression level of prognostic genes in the BRCA dataset. (B) KEGG analysis of the high- and low-risk groups. (C,D) Gene mutation frequency analysis in the high- (C) and low-risk groups (D). (E) Histogram of high- and low-risk group drug sensitivity analysis. (F) Correlations of PSME2, PSMD14 and PSMB8 with the IC50 values of chemotherapeutic drugs. ****, P<0.0001. BRCA, breast cancer; IC50, half-maximal inhibitory concentration; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes.

GSEA was used to reveal the pathways involved for both risk cohorts. The results revealed that these two risk cohorts were enriched in KEGG pathways such as allograft rejection, type I diabetes mellitus, antigen processing and presentation, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, and graft-versus-host disease ( Figure 4B ). The differential analysis of somatic mutations between the two risk cohorts revealed that the TP53 gene had the highest mutation rate in the high-risk cohort and the PIK3CA gene had the highest mutation rate in the low-risk cohort ( Figure 4C,4D ). Subsequent drug sensitivity analysis revealed IC50 information for 92 out of 138 drugs. Among these drugs, 73 exhibited significant IC50 discrepancies between the two risk cohorts, including CI.1040, GNF.2, roscovitine and AS601245 ( Figure 4E ). PSMB8 demonstrated the most robust negative relationship with roscovitine (R=−0.496), while PSMD14 maintained the strongest positive correlation with AS601245 (R=0.564) ( Figure 4F ).

In addition, the immune microenvironment landscape in the two risk cohorts was evaluated. The abundances of 22 kinds of immune cells in the samples of the two risk cohorts are illustrated in Figure 5A . There were 12 discrepant immune cells, of which M1 macrophages, CD8 + T-cells, resting myeloid dendritic cells (DCs), T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, gamma delta T cells, activated natural killer (NK) cells and regulatory T cells (Tregs) accounted for a greater proportion of the high-risk cohort; however, the proportions of M0 macrophages, naive B cells, M2 macrophages and activated/resting memory CD4 + T cells were the opposite ( Figure 5B ). In addition, M0 macrophages were significantly negatively correlated with resting myeloid DCs (R=−0.424) ( Figure 5C ). M1 macrophages and activated memory CD4 + T cells exhibited positive correlations with PSME2 and PSMB8 (|R|>0.3) ( Figure 5D ). Moreover, the expression levels of a total of 40 immune checkpoints were upregulated in the high-risk cohort (ADORA2A, BTLA, C10orf54, CD200, CD200R1, CD244, CD27, CD274, CD28, CD40, CD40LG, CD44, CD48, CD70, CD80, CD86, CTLA4, HHLA2, ICOS, IDO1, IDO2, KIR3DL1, LAG3, LAIR1, LGALS9, PDCD1, PDCD1LG2, SELPLG, TIGIT, TIMP3, TMIGD2, TNFRSF14, TNFRSF18, TNFRSF25, TNFRSF4, TNFRSF8, TNFRSF9, TNFSF14, TNFSF18 and TNFSF9) ( Figure 5E ). Spearman’s correlation analysis between prognostic genes and discrepant immune checkpoints revealed that PSME2 and PSMB8 were positively correlated with most immune checkpoints, whereas PSMD14 was poorly correlated with immune checkpoints ( Figure 5F ).

Immune landscape of the high- and low-risk groups. (A) Stacked graph of the proportions of various types of immune cells in the high- and low-risk groups. (B) Differences in the infiltration of immune cells between the high- and low-risk groups. (C) Correlation heatmap of differential immune cells. (D) Degree of correlation between differential immune cells and prognostic genes. (E) Differential expression of immune checkpoint genes between the high- and low-risk groups. (F) Degree of correlation between immune checkpoints and prognostic genes. (G) Differences in TIDE scores, dysfunction scores and exclusion scores between the high- and low-risk groups. *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001; ****, P<0.0001; ns, not significant. TIDE, tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion.

TIDE scores were evaluated to understand the immunoefficacy of the patients, and the results revealed that the reduced dysfunction score and elevated exclusion score in the high-risk cohort might indicate high immune rejection and poor immunotherapy efficacy in high-risk patients ( Figure 5G ).

The expression of three prognostic genes was quantified using RT-qPCR. The expression levels of PSME2 and PSMB8 were significantly higher in the control samples compared to the BRCA samples ( Figure 6A,6B ). Conversely, the expression level of PSMD14 was significantly elevated in the BRCA samples relative to the control samples ( Figure 6C ). Immunohistochemistry was utilized to evaluate the expression levels of these prognostic genes within BRCA tissues and paired control tissues. The results revealed that the expression level of PSMD14 was higher than that of PSME2 and PSMB8 ( Figure 6D ). Additionally, PSMD14 was knocked down in three different BRCA cell lines ( Figure S2 ). The CCK8 assay results indicated that PSMD14 significantly promotes the proliferation of BRCA cells ( Figure 6E ).

Validation of the expression and function of PSME2, PSMB8 and PSMD14 in breast cancer clinical samples and cell lines. (A) Analysis of PSME2 expression in BRCA tissues and paired control tissues by RT-qPCR. (B) Analysis of PSMB8 expression in BRCA tissues and paired control tissues by RT-qPCR. (C) Analysis of PSMD14 expression in BRCA tissues and paired control tissues by RT-qPCR. (D) Immunohistochemistry analysis of PSME2, PSMB8 and PSMD14 expression in BRCA tissues and paired control tissues. (E) CCK8 assay was carried out to detect the proliferation of control and PSMD14 knockdown BRCA cell lines. **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001. BRCA, breast cancer; CCK8, cell counting kit-8; RT-qPCR, real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction.
sections.discussion:
BRCA remains the most commonly diagnosed malignancy among women worldwide. Although the identification of specific biomarkers has improved the prognosis for BRCA patients by enabling early detection, the reliability of certain biomarkers is debated due to inconsistent predictive accuracy and conflicting results across different studies ( 21 ). Immunotherapies show considerable promise in improving tumor prognosis. Therefore, it is crucial to identify IRGs associated with BRCA to further develop targeted therapeutic strategies. The upregulation of the polyamine metabolic pathway has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various cancers, including BRCA ( 12 ). Nonetheless, few studies have examined the combined use of IRGs and polyamine metabolism pathway-related genes as prognostic markers for BRCA.

In this study, we identified PSME2 , PSMB8 , and PSMD14 as prognostic genes linked to immunity and polyamine metabolism in BRCA through bioinformatics analysis. Proteasome activator complex subunit 2 (PSME2), a member of the proteasome activator subunit gene family, plays a crucial role in proteasome-mediated protein degradation. It is upregulated in tumor tissues and is associated with an immuno-hot tumor immune microenvironment ( 22 ). These findings suggest its potential as a novel biomarker for characterizing the features of the tumor immune microenvironment and predicting responses to immunotherapy in patients with BRCA. Research has revealed a significant correlation between elevated immunoproteasome (ImP) expression and improved clinical outcomes, particularly among patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). This association is most pronounced when the expression of PSMB8 or PSMB9 is localized to tumor cells rather than stromal or immune cells. These findings suggest that PSMB8 may serve as a prognostic biomarker in BRCA patients ( 23 ). PSMD14, an integral component of the 19S regulatory subunits within the 26S proteasome complex, has emerged as a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in a range of human malignancies ( 24 ). A thorough review of the literature revealed an absence of reports connecting PSME2, PSMB8, PSMD14, and BRCA. Therefore, this study represents the inaugural identification of three prognostic genes associated with immune and polyamine metabolism in BRCA.

We subsequently constructed a risk model and a nomogram model to predict the prognosis of BRCA patients by assessing the expression levels of PSME2, PSMB8, and PSMD14. The performance evaluation results indicate that both models exhibit high accuracy in forecasting the prognosis of BRCA patients. The incorporation of LASSO regression alongside univariate and multivariate regression analyses for gene screening enhances the robustness of the study’s findings. GSEA, immune infiltration analysis, and drug sensitivity assays were utilized to investigate the enriched pathways in high-risk and low-risk cohorts and to evaluate the variations in immune infiltration and drug sensitivity among BRCA patients categorized by risk. The results revealed that the risk model, which is based on prognostic genes, along with the nomogram model, which integrates independent prognostic factors (risk score, T stage, N stage, and M stage), exhibited strong predictive accuracy for 1-, 2-, and 3-year survival probabilities in BRCA patients. The observed unfavorable prognosis and decreased survival time in the high-risk cohort may be attributed to the significant immune evasion capabilities of tumor cells in BRCA patients, alongside the limited effectiveness of immunotherapy within this subgroup.

While this study has yielded significant insights with the bioinformatics analysis of genes associated with BRCA, certain limitations remain. First, the findings are yet to be corroborated using a more extensive dataset and comparable platforms, potentially impacting the generalizability and reliability of the results. Second, although the mRNA and protein expression levels of PSME2, PSMB8, and PSMD14 have been assessed in BRCA tissue samples, and we identified the preliminary function of PSMD14 in BRCA cell lines. This study lacks additional experimental validation. Such validation is essential for confirming the molecular and cellular functions of PSME2, PSMB8, and PSMD14. Although bioinformatics analysis offers valuable insights into the potential prognostic significance of these genes, there remains a deficiency in the confirmation of their biological mechanisms through empirical experimentation. To substantiate these findings and enhance our understanding of the functional roles of these genes, we plan to perform experiments with animal models and perform Western blot analysis to observe the direct impact of these genes on tumor growth, metastasis, and treatment response. Concurrently, we will collect and analyze additional publicly available BRCA datasets to provide further opportunities for validation and exploration. Advanced single-cell sequencing technologies enable more precise resolution of immune cell heterogeneity, thereby elucidating the interactions among various immune cell subsets and prognostic genes. These subsequent studies are anticipated to address the limitations inherent in the current research and to provide a more comprehensive and profound understanding of the functions and prognostic significance of genes associated with BRCA.
sections.conclusion: In summary, we developed a prognostic regulatory network involving IRGs and polyamine metabolism associated with BRCA. Additionally, we introduced a risk model and a nomogram model, which have been identified as independent prognostic factors. Our findings contribute to the development of a potentially impactful framework for understanding and predicting BRCA patient outcomes.
